questions.learningObjective: detect which of the rhetorical situation's three questions a piece leaves open

stimulus.body: A short reference note on the rhetorical situation is set for a close-reading task. It states: A rhetorical situation answers who is speaking, to whom, and what is at stake now. A marginal reminder adds: look for an instruction to the reader anywhere in the three sentences. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The cue supplied for this item is “detect which of the rhetorical situation's three questions a piece leaves open / Look for an instruction to the reader anywhere…”. Which option follows from it?

options.text: What the writer wants the reader to do about the closure
Who the writer is speaking to and for
options.misconception: confuses the residents mentioned with the audience the piece never addresses

options.text: What makes the matter urgent at this moment
options.misconception: confuses the topic of the piece with the situation that makes it timely

options.text: How much the repair itself is likely to cost
options.misconception: turns a missing element of the situation into a missing figure

questions.explanation: A rhetorical situation answers who is speaking, to whom, and what is at stake now. This piece is clear on two counts: residents are the people concerned, and the vote and the August bill supply the urgency. What it never supplies is a request. It describes the closure, the bill and the silence about travel, and then stops, so a reader finishes informed and unasked, which is why the unanswered question is the one about what should happen next.
questions.hint: Look for an instruction to the reader anywhere in the three sentences.

stimulus.body: A short reference note on transitions that name a relation is set for a close-reading task. It states: The second sentence explains why the first sentence's consequence follows: the lorries crossing twice a shift are the reason the widening would cost more than it saves, and 'because' is the connective that says so. options.text: Although
options.misconception: reads the cost comparison as a concession that works against the first sentence

options.text: Because
For example

options.text: So that
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reasoning the passage sets out

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of an introduction that begins with a definition

stimulus.body: A short reference note on introductions from definition is set for a close-reading task. It states: An opening definition earns its place only if the reader can use it, which takes three steps before the thesis. A marginal reminder adds: ask what the reader needs before the thesis can be checked. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: Holding “sequence the moves of an introduction that begins with a definition / Ask what the reader needs before the thesis can be checked.…” in mind, which of the four options is correct?

options.text: State the thesis, so the reader knows what the term is being used to argue
options.misconception: leads with a conclusion the reader has no means of understanding yet

options.text: Name the term, so the reader has a word to hold on to
options.misconception: starts with an assertion that depends on the term being named first

options.text: Give a case the definition covers, so it is not left abstract
options.misconception: supplies illustration before the reader has been given the word

options.text: Show what the term does not settle, so the reader feels the need for a claim
options.misconception: reaches the limits of a term before the term has been given

questions.explanation: An opening definition earns its place only if the reader can use it, which takes three steps before the thesis. The word comes first, because nothing else can be said about a term the reader has never met. A case then shows the term doing work, and the limit follows, since a reader who has seen both an instance and the boundary of a definition is ready to hear what needs arguing. Placing the thesis at the end means the reader meets the claim already holding the tools to test it, which is why the other orders ask for judgement before they supply it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs before the thesis can be checked.

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about claims that name no one. the sentence has a group, a judgement and a claim of unanimity, and only two of those three can be weighed. It states: A paragraph built around a case runs rule, case, answer, limit, and each step is a precondition for the next. answer.exemplar: The first which can attach either to the signs or to the delivery, so a reader cannot tell whether the firm in the next county made the signs or arranged the delivery, which is a different supplier altogether. The second which most naturally attaches to the shortage, but can also be read as attaching to the delay, and on that reading the delay affected the region while the shortage was local. The cost of the first ambiguity is commercial, since making the signs and delivering them are different jobs done by different firms, and the cost of the second is factual, since a shortage with regional reach and a delay with regional reach are different claims. A good answer identifies both attachment points, gives the two readings for at least one, and repairs the sentence with a comma or a repeated noun rather than by deleting the information.
